headline: Five tickers, one incantation, no thesis required
lede: A social-media stock account lists five companies across telehealth, industrials, insurance, adtech, and bitcoin-mining-turned-AI infrastructure, and promises each has the potential to create "future millionaires." The breadth is the message — or rather, the breadth is a substitute for one.
body:
The post belongs to a recognizable genre on financial social media: the ticker litany. Five names, five identical verdicts, zero differentiation. The phrase "potential to create future millionaires" is not analysis; it is ritual, the secular equivalent of lighting candles before a shrine. It confers neither blame nor accountability — "potential" does a great deal of rhetorical heavy lifting — and it travels efficiently in a format hostile to nuance. What makes this particular list interesting is not the claim but the cast: these five companies share almost nothing except being publicly traded equities that have attracted retail enthusiasm at various points. Examining each on its actual merits produces a more complicated picture.

Hims & Hers Health (*HIMS*) built a genuine business in men's and women's personal-care subscriptions — hair loss, erectile dysfunction, skincare — then stumbled into a gold rush. During a prolonged shortage of *semaglutide*, the branded active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, US law permitted pharmacies to compound — that is, manufacture locally — their own versions at far lower prices. Hims made compounded semaglutide the centrepiece of its growth story, reporting $2.35 billion in full-year 2025 revenue. The FDA resolved the shortage in early 2025, legally ending that business, and the stock dropped roughly 20% in a week. The company has since pivoted: it now distributes branded Novo Nordisk drugs through its platform, acquired an Australian telehealth group for $1.15 billion, and launched a testosterone-therapy product. An SEC investigation into its GLP-1 marketing practices, disclosed in early 2026, adds regulatory texture to a narrative that is genuinely complicated — neither dead nor ascendant.

TE Connectivity (*TE*, NYSE: TEL) is an industrial-grade connector and sensor manufacturer with $18.7 billion in trailing revenue and a market capitalisation above $70 billion. It is not a speculative play in any conventional sense. Its connectors appear inside electric vehicles, high-voltage grid infrastructure, factory automation systems, and data-centre power distribution — invisible infrastructure for virtually every electrification megatrend. Analysts rate it a near-consensus "Strong Buy" and the company has raised its long-term organic growth target to 6–8% annually. If there is a "future millionaire" thesis here it is a slow-compounding one, driven by the sheer ubiquity of its components in the energy transition — not a short-squeeze or a product launch.

Oscar Health (*OSCR*) is a technology-oriented health insurer that operates exclusively on the Affordable Care Act individual marketplace, the government exchange for Americans without employer-sponsored insurance. It reached two million members by the end of 2025 and has a plausible path to operating profitability in 2026 after raising premiums roughly 28% year-over-year. The structural vulnerability is stark: approximately 93% of its premium revenue flows through federal advance tax credits. If Congress allows enhanced ACA subsidies to lapse, Oscar estimates the individual-insurance market could contract 20–30%. The bull case is real; so is the concentration of political risk in a single congressional vote.

Zeta Global (*ZETA*) operates what it markets as an AI marketing cloud — a data platform that aggregates consumer profiles to help large brands target and retain customers across digital channels. The company has reported 18 consecutive quarters of beating and raising its own guidance, with full-year 2025 revenue of $1.305 billion and a 2026 target of $1.785 billion. Net revenue retention of 120% suggests existing clients are spending more each year. The skeptic's question is durable: large data intermediaries are perpetually one privacy regulation or walled-garden expansion away from disruption, and the AI label, however genuinely applied, is shared with several hundred other companies currently seeking premium multiples.

IREN Limited (*IREN*), formerly Iris Energy, is perhaps the most dramatic transformation on the list. An Australian-founded, NASDAQ-listed renewable-energy bitcoin miner, it rebranded in late 2024 and signed a $9.7 billion, five-year cloud-computing agreement with Microsoft to deploy tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs from its power-rich Texas campuses. The stock rose roughly 285% in 2025. The thesis rests on a genuinely scarce asset — grid-connected land with secure power — and a credible anchor customer. The risks are execution-scale risks: the GPU deployment is ambitious, the competitive landscape for AI compute is intensifying, and the bitcoin-mining heritage means the company carries a perception discount from institutional investors who remain wary of the sector.

What unites these five companies, beyond the tweet, is that each carries a plausible long thesis alongside a specific, identifiable risk that is being elided. That elision is the work the "future millionaires" formula performs: it replaces the hard trade-off analysis — compounding regulatory exposure, subsidy dependency, margin compression, execution risk — with a generic aspiration. The list is not wrong, exactly. It is incomplete in ways that matter most to the people most likely to be moved by it.
fact_check: The tweet uses $TE; TE Connectivity trades on NYSE as TEL. Retail social media commonly abbreviates the ticker this way. All financial figures cited in the article (HIMS $2.35B 2025 revenue, IREN $9.7B Microsoft deal, ZETA 18 consecutive beat-and-raise quarters, OSCR ~93% premium revenue via federal credits, TE Connectivity $18.7B trailing revenue) are drawn from public filings, analyst reports, and news coverage as of early-to-mid 2026.
